item.title: People First emerges from FijiFirst’s collapse, says Seruiratu
item.description: The newly launched People First Party has its roots in the collapse of the FijiFirst Party, with leader Inia Seruiratu telling supporters that the new movement was formed to ensure thousands of former FijiFirst supporters were not left without political representation. item.content:encoded:
The newly launched People First Party has its roots in the collapse of the FijiFirst Party, with leader Inia Seruiratu telling supporters that the new movement was formed to ensure thousands of former FijiFirst supporters were not left without political representation.

Speaking at the party’s official launch in Nadi yesterday, Seruiratu said the deregistration of FijiFirst in July 2023 marked the end of one chapter in Fiji’s political history but created uncertainty for many supporters.

“Who are we? Let us look at the events that brought us here,” he said.

“We, the People First, are the remnants of the FijiFirst Party, which was officially deregistered around July 2023. That is now history.”

Seruiratu said the deregistration meant thousands of hardworking Fijians suddenly found themselves without the political party they had elected to represent them.

“Unfortunately, thousands of hardworking Fijians were disconnected and left without their chosen political representation overnight,” he said.

He said FijiFirst MPs subsequently became independent members of Parliament and were free to make their own political choices.

“As independent members of Parliament, we were free to make our own choices and go our own ways, which we did. But what happened to our voters?” he asked.

Seruiratu acknowledged the period following the party’s collapse was a difficult one but said it had provided valuable lessons that helped shape the formation of People First.

“We went through some challenging times, and the experience has taught us a lot of valuable lessons which can only help us in the future.”

He said party members faced considerable pressure during that period but chose to remain united rather than compromise the trust placed in them by supporters.

“Despite that, and the lure of lucrative office, we stood our ground. We refused to compromise the faith you placed in us.”

Seruiratu said the new party was founded on the principles of equality, integrity, respect and national unity.

“It was against that background that this new movement, People First, was formed,” he said.

item.title: FASA launches campaign backing $8 national living wage
item.description: The Federated Airline Staff Association (FASA) has launched a signature collection campaign in support of a proposed $8 national living wage, calling on its members to help gather public backing for the initiative. In a circular issued to members on July 30, FASA announced that the “$8 National Living Wage Campaign 2026 – Signature Collection” is now underway.
item.content:encoded:
The Federated Airline Staff Association (FASA) has launched a signature collection campaign in support of a proposed $8 national living wage, calling on its members to help gather public backing for the initiative.

In a circular issued to members on July 30, FASA announced that the “$8 National Living Wage Campaign 2026 – Signature Collection” is now underway.

The association is encouraging members to sign a petition advocating for what it describes as a fair and decent living wage. The signatures will form part of a petition to be submitted to the Government.

According to the circular, the campaign aims to collect 100,000 signatures nationwide.

FASA has urged members to play an active role in helping achieve the target, saying the campaign is aimed at improving living standards and promoting decent work for all workers.

Members wishing to support the campaign have been asked to visit the ATSET and FASA office to sign the petition.

The circular, signed by National Secretary Rimal Kumar, thanked members for their continued support and solidarity as the campaign gets underway.

item.title: People First party announces provisional candidates
item.description: THE People First Party announced its 15 provisional candidate list yesterday at Korovuto in Nadi ahead of the general election. The provisional lineup includes Kalesi Toga, Sitiveni Weleilakeba, Ashley Amrita Singh, Arisi Tabuasei, Luisa Vusonimasei, Mohammed Saiyaz Khan, Apakuki Nalaukai, Sushila Rameshwar, Ravina Lata, Jasmine Lal, Ashneel Sudhakar, Ali Sheikh, Adi Laisa Tora, and Hazrat Ali.
item.content:encoded:
THE People First Party announced its 15 provisional candidate list yesterday at Korovuto in Nadi ahead of the general election.

The provisional lineup includes Kalesi Toga, Sitiveni Weleilakeba, Ashley Amrita Singh, Arisi Tabuasei, Luisa Vusonimasei, Mohammed Saiyaz Khan, Apakuki Nalaukai, Sushila Rameshwar, Ravina Lata, Jasmine Lal, Ashneel Sudhakar, Ali Sheikh, Adi Laisa Tora, and Hazrat Ali.

Addressing supporters, party leader Inia Seruiratu expressed gratitude for the ongoing backing from the community and acknowledged the pressing national concerns facing citizens.

“We do not have a party manifesto as we speak because we first need to consult and hear you,” he said.

“We are people first, your choices and proposals are important in the formulation of our party manifesto.”

Party president Joana Koroilavesau emphasized that the movement’s foundation was rooted in grassroots representation rather than personal ambition.

“We were not driven by power, position or privilege. We were driven by a simple conviction,” she said.

“With the voice of every day, teachers deserve to be heard, respected and represented. We have welcomed people from every corner of life, every community, every faith and every background.”

In addition to the provisional group, the party confirmed its board of governors lineup. The confirmed candidates running for the general election are Joseph Nand, Virendra Lal, Hem Chand, Vijay Nath, Semi Koroilavesau, Alvick Maharaj, Rinesh Sharma, and Parveen Bala Kumar.

Mr Seruiratu confirmed provisional candidates will still complete formal vetting procedures.

item.title: Ministry vows change after sea ordeal
item.description: THE Ministry of Health will act on lessons learned from the Lau sea ordeal, with Assistant Minister for Health Penioni Ravunawa acknowledging the response comes only after the incident. Responding to questions on why transport arrangements for health workers travelling to maritime communities had not been reviewed earlier, Mr Ravunawa said the ministry would now address the issues exposed by the i
item.content:encoded:
THE Ministry of Health will act on lessons learned from the Lau sea ordeal, with Assistant Minister for Health Penioni Ravunawa acknowledging the response comes only after the incident.

Responding to questions on why transport arrangements for health workers travelling to maritime communities had not been reviewed earlier, Mr Ravunawa said the ministry would now address the issues exposed by the incident.

“Although being reactive, it is better that we do something about it now to prevent a similar incident in the future,” he said.

Mr Ravunawa said the ordeal had exposed critical gaps and provided valuable lessons for the ministry.

“This incident has brought in a lot of learning lessons.”

He said Health Minister Dr Atonio Lalabalavu would brief Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka on the incident and outline areas requiring urgent improvement.

“The minister is having a briefing with the Prime Minister to highlight some of the gaps and how we can improve looking after our staff who are serving in the maritime communities.”

Mr Ravunawa said the ministry was committed to ensuring health workers travelling to remote maritime areas had access to safer transport.

He said this was particularly important in the Lau Group, where islands are widely dispersed and health workers often travel long distances by sea to deliver essential services.

“It is important that we try and get a boat that is safe for them to be able to reach to their community in a safe manner.”

The six health workers were rescued after being stranded at sea for more than 30 hours while on an outreach program in the Lau Group.

Mr Ravunawa said the incident had provided an opportunity for the ministry to closely examine the challenges faced by staff delivering healthcare services to Fiji’s maritime communities.

THE six-member medical team rescued from Lau waters received medical treatment at Tamavua Twomey Hospital yesterday after returning to Viti Levu.

The team arrived at Nausori Airport from Lakeba on a chartered flight at about 2pm, where they were welcomed by Health Minister Dr Atonio Lalabalavu before being transported by ambulance to Twomey Hospital for medical assessment and care.

The Fiji Times followed the medical team to the hospital but was instructed to leave the premises as medical protocols were in place.

Later, members of the medical and nursing fraternity gathered to honour their colleagues’ determination and reflect on their ordeal after they spent more than 30 hours at sea.

The service, themed Together in Faith, United in Prayer had originally been organised as a prayer gathering for the missing team.

However, by 3pm yesterday, it had become a thanksgiving service celebrating the safe return of the six survivors.

The opening prayer was led by Chaplain Dr Ledua Tamani and Senikuba Qolisese.

During the service, Dr Tamani said the medical team had given their best in serving communities in the Lau Group, and God had brought them home safely.

“We extend much gratitude to the boat master who held steady, the steadfast faith of those who prayed without ceasing, and above all, the Lord whose protection never fails,” Dr Tamani said

item.title: Defence pact focuses on external threats
item.description: AUSTRALIA says its new defence alliance with Fiji is aimed solely at responding to external threats and does not provide for military intervention during domestic political instability. In an interview with The Fiji Times online portal, The Lens@177, Australian High Commissioner to Fiji Peter Roberts clarified the scope of the Veitacini Alliance, signed alongside the Vuvale Union.
item.content:encoded:
AUSTRALIA says its new defence alliance with Fiji is aimed solely at responding to external threats and does not provide for military intervention during domestic political instability.

In an interview with The Fiji Times online portal, The Lens@177, Australian High Commissioner to Fiji Peter Roberts clarified the scope of the Veitacini Alliance, signed alongside the Vuvale Union.

“Our Prime Minister has actually signed two agreements, the Vuvala Union and also the Veitacini Alliance or Ocean of Peace Alliance.

“The Vuvale Union is a cross-cutting agreement saying we’ll co-operate in a whole bunch of areas and that has this work plan that comes with it.

“And the Veitacini Alliance is saying we’ll become allies to each other and that means we’re saying if one of us was attacked or we faced a threat then the other would come to support.

“So, Australia only has this alliance relationship with three countries and Fiji would be the fourth.

“That just means, you’d think this never would need to be applied but if one of us was under threat, we’d be ready to stand there with each other.”

When asked whether Australian troops would be deployed if Fiji experienced internal instability, Mr Roberts said:

“That’s right. It’s a treaty between two countries and it talks about if other parties come and threaten.

“The treaty doesn’t talk about that sort of thing. It’s a treaty between Fiji and Australia about how we deal with threats that come into the Pacific.”

item.title: Australia prioritises transnational crime prevention
item.description: AUSTRALIA has identified transnational crime, particularly the growing flow of illicit drugs through the Pacific, as the biggest priority under its new Vuvale Union with Fiji, with additional police resources, infrastructure support and intelligence co-operation planned over the next decade. In an interview with The Fiji Times online portal, The Lens@177, Australian High Commissioner to Fiji Peter
item.content:encoded:
AUSTRALIA has identified transnational crime, particularly the growing flow of illicit drugs through the Pacific, as the biggest priority under its new Vuvale Union with Fiji, with additional police resources, infrastructure support and intelligence co-operation planned over the next decade.

In an interview with The Fiji Times online portal, The Lens@177, Australian High Commissioner to Fiji Peter Roberts said drug trafficking had emerged as one of the region’s most pressing security challenges.

“I think we all want to do more because this is a growing challenge,” he said.

“To be honest, five years ago we wouldn’t have said this was going to be the challenge it was.

“These drug dealers change the routes that they bring drugs according to circumstances and we’ve definitely seen it pick up in the Pacific.

“So I think it’s not Fiji, it’s not Australia, it’s everybody in the region. We all have to be doing more to address this.”

Mr Roberts said tackling the growing flow of illicit drugs was one of the most significant priorities under the Vuvale Union.

“This is probably the biggest individual component in Vuvale Union, be it supporting maritime surveillance, be it the work we do with the RFMF already on the patrol boats that Australia supports, be it in supporting incorporation of sharing information and forensic work as Fiji Police follow leads.

“We’ve got to have across-the-board co-operation and that’s a key pillar of Vuvale Union.

“I should also say, drugs is not just about catching the criminals, it’s also about how we deal with it as a society.”

He also said there was still considerable work to be done in the health sector.

“We’re seeing the issue of HIV emerge and how our communities respond and we’re sharing experiences and how we deal with this in Australia and how Fiji deals with it and there’s lots of opportunities to share there.”

item.title: Roberts dismisses China rivalry claims
item.description: AUSTRALIA has dismissed suggestions its expanding partnership with Fiji is aimed at countering China’s influence in the Pacific, insisting the relationship is driven by shared interests and regional co-operation. In an interview with The Fiji Times online portal, The Lens@177, Australian High Commissioner to Fiji Peter Roberts said Australia’s focus was on strengthening its long-standing relations
item.content:encoded:
AUSTRALIA has dismissed suggestions its expanding partnership with Fiji is aimed at countering China’s influence in the Pacific, insisting the relationship is driven by shared interests and regional co-operation.

In an interview with The Fiji Times online portal, The Lens@177, Australian High Commissioner to Fiji Peter Roberts said Australia’s focus was on strengthening its long-standing relationship with Fiji.

“I think where Australia is coming from, we just want to be the best possible partner for Fiji that we can be, because we believe that it makes sense for Fiji and Australia to work together,” Mr Roberts said.

“So, when we talk about the co-operation we do with Fiji, it’s because it makes sense for Australia, it makes sense for Fiji, and I hope it makes sense for the region when we work together for the region.

Mr Roberts said Australia wanted to deepen co-operation across economic development, regional security and people-to-people ties through the Vuvale Union.

item.title: Tabuya praises recycling as economic opportunity
item.description: TURNING waste into products such as toilet paper while reducing the amount of rubbish ending up in landfills shows how recycling can drive economic growth while protecting the environment, says Minister for Environment and Climate Change Lynda Tabuya. Speaking at the 15th anniversary celebration of South Pacific Waste Recyclers in Suva on Wednesday, Ms Tabuya said the company had demonstrated that
item.content:encoded:
TURNING waste into products such as toilet paper while reducing the amount of rubbish ending up in landfills shows how recycling can drive economic growth while protecting the environment, says Minister for Environment and Climate Change Lynda Tabuya.

Speaking at the 15th anniversary celebration of South Pacific Waste Recyclers in Suva on Wednesday, Ms Tabuya said the company had demonstrated that waste could become a valuable resource through responsible management.

“For the past fifteen years, your work has helped divert valuable recyclable materials away from landfills, reduced pollution, created employment opportunities, and shown that waste has value when managed responsibly,” she said.

“You have demonstrated that what many consider waste can become a valuable resource.”

She said the approach reflected the principles of a circular economy, where materials were kept in use through reuse, repair and recycling instead of the traditional take, make and dispose model.

She added Fiji continued to face increasing waste management challenges driven by population growth, urbanisation, tourism and changing consumption patterns, placing greater pressure on landfills and the environment.

Ms Tabuya said Government had finalised the National Waste Management and Pollution Control Strategy 2026-2035 and was progressing the Container Deposit Regulations to introduce a refund system for beverage containers.

“Their success depends on implementation, innovation, and more importantly, partnerships.”

“That is why Government greatly values companies such as South Pacific Waste Recyclers, whose investments and expertise help turn policy into practical action.”

Minister for Information, Environment and Climate Change Lynda Tabuya at the South Pacific Waste Recyclers warehouse in Laucala Beach, in Nasinu on Wednesday. Picture: JONACANI LALAKOBAU
